note: Judgement on which parent is principal. The sources name cuplé (no id in the tree) as the form copla grew out of, and list tonadilla, variety theatre, zarzuela and ópera flamenca as antecedents; zarzuela is the antecedent with an id and the model for copla's orchestral accompaniment. If the lead adds cuplé, it should be the principal parent and zarzuela 'other'.
Ópera flamenca is a named antecedent and copla's texture is 'aflamencada, sin jondura'. Not principal: copla is orchestral theatre song, not cante.

Pasodoble is one of the rhythms copla is written in (Carmen de España, Campanera); the tree's pasodoble record already covers the sung pasodoble canción by the same singers. Judgement: no source states descent.

Judgement. The sources present dōyō as a deliberate replacement for and reaction against Monbushō shōka, and as a separate concept; none states descent. It is the nearest existing genre: the same Western-style children's song idiom, the same schools and some of the same composers (Nakayama Shinpei began as a school shōka teacher, not in our claims).

Sourced: punto has 'Andalusian and Canary Islands origins' and took the décima espinela, quatrain coplas and the laúd from the Canaries. iberianpop is the tree's record for Iberian song with décima verse; it ends in 1800 and names Seville, so it fits the Andalusian side better than the Canarian. A Canary Islands folk record does not exist.

English Wikipedia (citing Manuel, Caribbean Currents, p. 156): twoubadou 'combined music derived from the guajiro traditions of Cuba' with méringue, brought back by Haitian cane cutters. The claim is checked as far as Wikipedia goes; the book itself was not read. Says 'guajiro traditions', not guitar style specifically. Twoubadou keeps son as principal parent.

Sourced: the punto, known in Spain as 'punto de La Habana', was taken into flamenco in the second half of the 19th century as the palo called guajira (a return trip; flamenco's own principal parent is unchanged).

Judgement. Chinese Wikipedia says nanguan carries the aesthetic of ancient yayue and is close to the Tang qingyue daqu court suites; no source states descent from the Zhou ritual music our yayue record describes. Nearest existing id; the closer ancestors (xianghe ge, qingshang yue, Tang daqu) have no id.

Ben Jones (2024) calls tagroupit a Tamazight-language sub-genre of the 1970s 'bands phenomenon' (Dhahira) that Nass El Ghiwane started; Ousmane and Izenzaren formed in its wake, the early Izenzaren closer to Ghiwani folk. Stated by the sources, not a judgement.

The bands reworked rrways poems (Ousmane cited Hadj Belaid and others) and the later fusion bands built on rways and the ribab. That the bands descend from rways is stated for repertoire; making it 'other' rather than 'principal' is a judgement, since the sources describe the bands as a break with the ribab-and-naqus sound.
Judgement: only one press source (on Amarg Fusion) names ahwash rhythms as a basis; no source states descent for the 1970s bands.

Judgement: the nearest existing id for an African root. Brito calls batuque 'de origem africana'; Gonçalves (via pt Wikipedia) says it is not a transplanted continental genre but an adaptation of some African dance that developed its own character in Cape Verde. No source names a parent genre in the tree.

proposal: alias and marker of batuku, not a separate record
note: Finaçon is the improvised verse sung inside a batuku session, in the batuku rhythm, by the lead singer (en Wikipedia; Brito 1998). Recordings labelled finaçon (Ntóni Denti d'Oru, Nha Mita Pereira, Nácia Gomi) are batuku circle recordings. Represent it as an alias and the second marker, not a child genre. Caution: the 1980s-90s band Finaçon played funaná, so the alias must not pull that band's songs into batuku.

proposal: separate record later (sibling under n_capeverdeanmusic), not a child of batuku
note: Tabanka is a different Santiago (and Maio) tradition: a May-July procession and mutual-aid association with drums, conch shells and cornets in a fast binary rhythm, banned from the late 19th century. No source makes it a form of batuku; they share only island, colonial bans and the revival composers (Pantera wrote a 'Tabanca'). Give it its own record (id 'tabanka', proposed parent wadrum, judgement) in a later round; until then do not fold it into batuku.
